conversation.content:
Hi there—thank you for coming in today. I’m Dr. Walker, a perinatal mental-health clinician, and I’m here to check in on how you’re feeling now that your baby has arrived. We’ll be using a short questionnaire called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS for short. It’s simply a 10-question screen that helps us see how mood, anxiety, and energy levels can shift after childbirth. Anything you share stays between us unless you or your baby’s safety is at immediate risk, and there are no right or wrong answers—just whatever feels true for you over the past seven days. We’ll move through the questions together; each one only takes a moment. Ready to begin?

First, thinking about the past week: have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt hard to do lately?

I’ve laughed a little, but mostly it feels forced. Sometimes my partner cracks a joke and I try to smile because I know he’s trying to cheer me up, but the laughter doesn’t come easily. I’d say it’s been harder than usual—like the joy is buried under a heavy blanket.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Sometimes I can, but it’s not the same. My sister sent me a funny video yesterday and I chuckled for a second, then felt guilty for even enjoying it when I’m supposed to be focused on the baby. Most days, though, nothing feels funny—everything feels flat and gray.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really. I used to get excited about little stuff—coffee with a friend, a walk to the park—but now I mostly think, “What’s the point?” I still go through the motions so people don’t worry, yet the spark just isn’t there.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah, I do that a lot. If she fusses for more than a few minutes, I immediately think it’s because I’m not comforting her right or because I ate something that upset my breast milk. Last night she wouldn’t settle, and I lay there convinced it was my fault for not being “in tune” enough with her needs. I know in my head that babies just cry, but the guilty loop keeps running.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be feeding her and suddenly imagine she’s stopped breathing, so I’m constantly checking her chest rise. Or I worry the stroller brake will fail and she’ll roll into the street. There’s no real reason—it’s like my mind won’t let me believe she’s safe unless I’m on high alert.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yes, sometimes it hits out of nowhere. My heart races, I feel sweaty, and I imagine something awful is about to happen—even if I’m just sitting on the couch with her asleep in the bassinet. It passes after a few minutes, but in the moment I feel like I have to jump up and check on her or call someone just to be sure everything’s okay.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days they do. When she won’t nap and the laundry’s piled up, it feels like I’m drowning. I pace with her in one arm and a burp cloth in the other, thinking, “How does anyone do this?” I still push through—she gets fed, the diapers get changed—but inside I’m running on fumes and tears.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yes. I lie down exhausted, but my head keeps spinning—replay- ing every little thing I might have done wrong, worrying she’ll wake up screaming, or just feeling this heavy sadness. Some nights I drift off okay, then jolt awake for no reason and can’t settle again. I probably get three or four broken hours in total, and even when she’s sleeping I can’t seem to shut my eyes properly.
I have felt sad or miserable

That’s most of my day, honestly. I wake up with this dull ache in my chest, and it just lingers. Little things—seeing a cute onesie, hearing a lullaby—can make me tear up. People keep telling me these weeks are supposed to be joyful, but mostly I feel like I’m watching it all through a fog.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah. I’ve cried three, maybe four times this week—usually when I’m alone with her during the long afternoon stretch. Once it was because I couldn’t get her to latch, another time just because the house felt so quiet and I felt so empty. The tears come without warning, and once they start it’s hard to stop.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, I haven’t thought about hurting myself. When I feel overwhelmed, I think about running away for an hour—just driving to the grocery store alone—but never anything like harming myself.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 24: Postpartum Depression Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Patient-reported symptoms (10-item EPDS-style inquiry):

1. <sym>Anhedonia</sym>: marked reduction in ability to experience joy or humor; describes mood as “flat and gray.”  
2. <sym>Loss of interest/anticipation</sym>: reports “What’s the point?” regarding previously enjoyable activities.  
3. <sym>Excessive guilt</sym>: recurrent self-blame for infant fussiness; believes she is “not in tune” enough.  
4. <sym>Generalized anxiety</sym>: daily intrusive worries about infant safety (breathing, stroller brake).  
5. <sym>Panic-like episodes</sym>: sudden racing heart, sweating, dread “out of nowhere” while infant is safe.  
6. <sym>Feeling overwhelmed</sym>: describes “drowning,” functioning on “fumes and tears.”  
7. <sym>Mood-related insomnia</sym>: difficulty initiating and maintaining sleep despite exhaustion; ruminates on perceived mistakes.  
8. <sym>Persistent dysphoria</sym>: “dull ache in chest… watching through a fog.”  
9. <sym>Frequent crying spells</sym>: 3–4×/week, unpredictable onset.  
10. <sym>Self-harm ideation</sym>: denied; passive urge to briefly leave scene when overwhelmed, but no suicidal or self-injury thoughts.

Pattern: Symptoms present most days and interfere with functioning; onset within weeks post-delivery.  
Risk factors: primiparous, sleep deprivation, high self-expectations, no apparent psychosocial support beyond family check-ins.

Safety: No self-harm or suicidal ideation reported; no plan or intent.

Screening impression: High clinical concern for <med>major postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety</med>; score estimation ≥12 on standard EPDS. Recommend formal diagnostic assessment and discussion of evidence-based treatment options.
